documents.title: Academic Policies: Artificial Intelligence and Generative AI section
documents.summary: This page gives the university AI wording for students: AI is not banned or allowed as a whole, but "Instructors have the right to specify if, when, and how AI may be used", and students must follow each syllabus. It adds acknowledgment, verification and misconduct expectations. Only one section of a long policies page is about AI.
documents.stance_why: The text sets no default stance. It says "Instructors have the right to specify if, when, and how AI may be used in their classes" and tells students to "check every syllabus", so the decision is handed to instructors (delegates). It offers no tiers.

units.why: The opening sentence frames the whole section: "a rapidly changing technology that is creating both new opportunities and challenges". It sets purpose and principles for AI at the institution, so P56 (framework preamble) fits; it states no rule itself.
units.anchor: generative artificial intelligence is a rapidly changing technology that is creating both new opportunities and

units.why: "Transparency and accountability are expected" states a principle for all users of generative AI rather than a specific step, so it is a university-level principle (P56); the concrete disclosure duty comes in a later sentence (P24).
units.anchor: Transparency and accountability are expected with the use of generative AI.

units.why: "Instructors have the right to specify if, when, and how AI may be used in their classes" gives the decision to each instructor rather than setting a university-wide ban or permission, so P04 fits.
units.anchor: Instructors have the right to specify if, when, and how AI may be used in

units.why: "You should always check every syllabus for clarification and policies" makes the student responsible for finding out each course's AI rules, which is P78 (not P10, which is about asking when unsure).
units.anchor: You should always check every syllabus for clarification and policies on how you may or
units.policy: Students always check every syllabus for how they may or may not use generative AI in coursework.

units.why: "Contact your instructor if that information is not available in the syllabus" tells students to ask the instructor when the syllabus is silent, which is P10 (ask when unsure).
units.anchor: Contact your instructor if that information is not available in the syllabus

units.why: "students will provide appropriate acknowledgment of their AI use" when AI is allowed is a disclosure duty with submissions, so P24; the condition "when AI is allowed" keeps it permissive.
units.anchor: when AI is allowed, students will provide appropriate acknowledgment of their AI use

units.why: The comparison "just as we require appropriate citations and references for any sources" treats AI acknowledgment like source citation under existing rules. P45 is the nearest type, though the analogy is to sources, not to a human collaborator.
units.anchor: just as we require appropriate citations and references for any sources
units.fit_note: The analogy is to cited sources, not to a human collaborator.

units.why: "expected to check any information generated by an AI platform for inaccuracies" because AI "can produce incorrect information" tells students to verify AI output, P31; "generally" softens it to should.
units.anchor: AI users are also generally expected to check any information generated by an AI platform

units.why: "Improper use of generative AI ... is a form of academic misconduct and subject to student sanctions" classifies misuse as misconduct handled by integrity processes (P36); it ties misuse to the university policy or the instructor's rules.
units.anchor: is a form of academic misconduct and subject to student sanctions

documents.title: Instructor Requirements and Resources: Artificial Intelligence and Generative AI section
tiers: Use is freely permitted with no acknowledgment
documents.summary: The instructor page repeats the university AI statement and tells faculty to put AI guidelines in the syllabus at the start of the course. It adds questions for drafting a syllabus statement and sample language in four options from freely permitted to prohibited.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no single rule: faculty are "responsible for communicating their AI guidelines" and it supplies sample statements ranging from "Use is freely permitted" to "Use prohibited". Because it offers options and hands the choice to instructors, the stance is delegates, with the four options as tiers.

units.why: The opening sentence frames the section: "a rapidly changing technology that is creating both new opportunities and challenges". It is a purpose statement (P56), not a rule.

units.anchor: Transparency and accountability are expected with the use of generative AI.

units.why: "UNLV expects that students will provide appropriate acknowledgment when using generative AI" is a duty to disclose AI use in submitted work, so P24.

units.why: "students are generally expected to check any information generated by an AI platform for inaccuracies" is a verification duty, P31, softened by "generally".

units.why: "Improper use of generative AI ... is a form of academic misconduct" classifies misuse under integrity rules, P36, whether the rule comes from the university policy or the instructor.

units.why: "Faculty are responsible for communicating their AI guidelines to students at the beginning of the course and embedding them within the course syllabus" is a mandatory syllabus AI statement, P09.

units.anchor: should align with the norms of transparency and accountability of your discipline
units.fit_note: Instructor guidance should align with discipline norms and unit-level AI policies; it does not say units may set their own rules.

units.why: "Does your statement cover different types of assignments, i.e., tests, essays, presentations, group work" prompts instructors to set AI rules per assignment type, closest to P04 (rule set per assignment).
units.anchor: Does your statement cover different types of assignments, i.e., tests, essays, presentations, group work
units.policy: Instructors consider whether the syllabus AI statement covers different types of assignments (tests, essays, presentations, group work).
units.fit_note: Phrased as a question to consider; it prompts coverage by assignment type rather than stating that rules differ.

units.policy: Instructors consider asking students to verify or check sources of information used by an AI tool when possible.

units.why: "ensure that all students have access to tools and support for learning about steering generative AI and critically analyzing output" is an equity-of-access prompt for instructors, P51.

units.policy: Instructors consider how they will ensure all students have access to tools and support for learning about steering generative AI and critically analyzing output.

units.why: The section "Sample Syllabus Language Options for AI-use" groups sample statements under "Encouraging the Use of AI" and "Discouraging the Use of AI" with named options (freely permitted, with acknowledgment, with prior permission, prohibited). That is a set of named tiers, P05.
units.anchor: Sample Syllabus Language Options for AI-use
units.policy: UNLV offers sample syllabus AI language in named options: use freely permitted with no acknowledgment, use only with acknowledgment, use only with prior permission, and use prohibited.

units.why: The sample option "Use is freely permitted" says students "are allowed to use advanced automated tools" and "no special documentation or citation is required". That is a default-permit statement, P02, and it also drops disclosure.
units.anchor: Students are allowed to use advanced automated tools on learning activities in this course
units.policy: Students are allowed to use advanced automated tools on learning activities in this course; no special documentation or citation is required.

units.why: The sample option "Use only with acknowledgment" allows AI "if that use is properly documented and credited", a disclosure condition on permitted use. P24 is the single type chosen; P02 does not capture the condition.
units.anchor: if that use is properly documented and credited
units.policy: Students are allowed to use advanced automated generative AI tools on learning activities in this course if that use is properly documented and credited.

units.why: "Students are welcome to use AI tools as supplementary resources" is a welcoming sample statement, P02, bounded by "does not circumvent authentic learning".
units.anchor: Students are welcome to use AI tools as supplementary resources to assist with learning activities

units.why: "Cite any AI tools properly, following the citation style specified by the faculty member" requires citing AI use in the sample statement, P24; it names no tool, prompt or output details (so not P25).
units.anchor: Cite any AI tools properly, following the citation style specified by the faculty member

units.why: "Not use AI tools to replace independent thinking, analysis or engagement with course content" keeps the student as the primary thinker, P32.
units.anchor: Not use AI tools to replace independent thinking, analysis or engagement with course content

units.why: "Provide evidence of how the AI tool contributed to the learning activity, including what the student learned ... how its accuracy and reliability were verified" asks for a written account of AI use, which is a reflection requirement, P26.
units.anchor: Provide evidence of how the AI tool contributed to the learning activity

units.why: "Consult with their professor before submitting work if there are any questions about what constitutes acceptable use" tells students to ask when unsure, P10.
units.anchor: Consult with their professor before submitting work if there are any questions about what constitutes

units.anchor: Unless permitted to use generative AI tools, each student is expected to complete each assignment

units.why: "Use AI tools to support learning, and not simply to generate assignments, discussion board posts, essays, presentations" bars having AI produce submitted work, P19.
units.anchor: not simply to generate assignments, discussion board posts, essays, presentations, etc.

units.anchor: Students are not allowed to use advanced automated generative AI tools on learning activities in

units.policy: Students do not use any generative AI tools, such as chatbots, text generators, paraphrasers, summarizers, or solvers, to complete any part of their coursework.

units.why: The Teaching & Learning Commons offers a "Faculty Resources course" with resources on "AI in the classroom", which supports instructors in learning about AI (P63).
units.anchor: helpful resources spanning various topics such as AI in the classroom, instructional strategies, and online

documents.title: AI Best Practices
documents.summary: UNLV IT says there is no AI-specific campus policy and that existing policies already apply. It offers best practices on treating AI like human help, acknowledging use, protecting data, choosing tools and checking output for bias and errors.
documents.stance_why: The page allows AI use with conditions: "Generative AI should be treated analogously to assistance from another person" and one "should acknowledge the use of generative AI", with data protection and verification duties. It is not a course policy and bans nothing outright, so permit with conditions.

units.why: "no UNLV-wide policies have been outlined relating to AI assessment, grading, content creation, or general use across campus" states the absence of an institution-wide AI policy. No type covers this, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: no UNLV-wide policies have been outlined relating to AI assessment, grading, content creation, or general
units.uncovered_note: States that UNLV has no campus-wide AI policy on assessment, grading, content creation or general use.

units.why: "UNLV faculty, staff, and students are required to adhere to NSHE and institutional policies and procedures" is a duty to follow existing policy, P77.
units.anchor: required to adhere to NSHE and institutional policies and procedures

units.why: "existing university policies already encompass the use of AI technologies" says AI use falls under existing policies (IT, privacy, academic misconduct), P77.
units.anchor: existing university policies already encompass the use of AI technologies

units.why: "Generative AI should be treated analogously to assistance from another person" treats AI like a human helper under existing rules, P45.
units.anchor: Generative AI should be treated analogously to assistance from another person

units.why: "Using generative AI tools to complete a Financial or Human Capital Management project, or entering assignment or exam answers is not advisable" discourages these uses without forbidding them, P03.
units.anchor: or entering assignment or exam answers is not advisable

units.why: "Personally identifiable information, system credentials (passwords, IP addresses), and non-public records should not be provided as prompts" protects confidential data, P50.
units.anchor: should not be provided as prompts

units.why: "One should acknowledge the use of generative AI (other than incidental use)" is a disclosure rule with an exemption for incidental use. P24 is chosen; the incidental-use exemption is not fully captured.
units.anchor: One should acknowledge the use of generative AI (other than incidental use)
units.fit_note: Excludes incidental use from the acknowledgment duty.

units.why: "default to disclosing such assistance when in doubt" tells people to err toward disclosure when unsure. P10 is the nearest (when unsure), though it directs disclosure instead of asking.
units.anchor: default to disclosing such assistance when in doubt
units.fit_note: When unsure, the instruction is to disclose rather than to ask the instructor.

units.why: "Avoid inputting sensitive or personal information into AI systems" protects personal data, P50.
units.anchor: Avoid inputting sensitive or personal information into AI systems

units.why: "Restrict the permissions granted to AI applications to only what is necessary" limits what access AI tools get. It protects data and security (P50), but it is about tool permissions rather than personal data.
units.anchor: Restrict the permissions granted to AI applications to only what is necessary for their functionality
units.fit_note: Concerns limiting permissions granted to AI applications, not personal data.

units.why: "Contact UNLV IT if needing to integrate AI into university applications to ensure compliance with data security and privacy requirements" routes AI integration through IT review, which is nearest P65 (review of AI tools before deployment).
units.anchor: Contact UNLV IT if needing to integrate AI into university applications
units.fit_note: Asks users to contact IT; it does not describe a formal approval process.

units.why: "Review AI outputs for malicious content, appropriateness, accessibility, bias or discriminatory outputs" asks users to evaluate AI output critically, P31.
units.anchor: Review AI outputs for malicious content, appropriateness, accessibility, bias or discriminatory outputs

units.why: "Always employ human judgment when using AI outputs" keeps people as the decision-makers, nearest P32; it is not limited to students solving problems.
units.anchor: Always employ human judgment when using AI outputs
units.fit_note: Applies to all users of AI output and not only to a student's problem-solving.

units.why: "Enterprise tools are computer applications, software, hardware, or systems that are supported by UNLV" defines the term that sets which tools the guidance covers, P61.
units.anchor: Enterprise tools are computer applications, software, hardware, or systems that are supported by UNLV

units.why: "Supported tools include data agreements and other protections for institutional data and content" explains why UNLV-supported tools are safer, which supports preferring vetted tools (P50).
units.anchor: Supported tools include data agreements and other protections for institutional data and content

units.why: "Review their privacy policies" for third-party tools is a must-do ("it is imperative that you") to protect data, P50.
units.anchor: Carefully read and understand the privacy policies of the AI tool

units.why: "Check security measures" such as encryption for third-party tools is a data-protection step, P50.
units.anchor: Ensure the tool has robust security measures in place, such as encryption and secure data

units.why: "Use AI tools from reputable and trusted providers" prefers vetted tools, P50.
units.anchor: Use AI tools from reputable and trusted providers and verify the legitimacy of the tool

units.why: "Only provide the minimum necessary data to the AI tool" limits data shared with third-party tools, P50.
units.anchor: Only provide the minimum necessary data to the AI tool

units.why: "AI models can output biased or discriminatory results" names bias as a concern, P53, as a fact and not a rule.
units.anchor: AI models can output biased or discriminatory results

units.why: "Users are ultimately responsible for verifying the output they utilize from AI is free of discrimination, bias" places verification duty on users, P31.
units.anchor: Users are ultimately responsible for verifying the output they utilize from AI is free of

units.why: "AI can also provide inaccurate or misleading information" and "it is up to the user to verify the accuracy" is a verification duty for accuracy, P31.
units.anchor: it is up to the user to verify the accuracy of the AI outputs

notes: Coder A. Three university-level documents; no school or computing-unit policy found (see collect file). Students and instructors pages share the same AI paragraph, coded separately per document. IT page is practice guidance, not a coursework policy. Non-AI page content (classroom recording, DRC, etc.) was skipped.
